content: Preparing the cervix before a first-trimester surgical abortion is intended to make the procedure both safer and easier. There are two main approaches to cervical preparation: the use of osmotic dilators and pharmacologic agents. Various formulations and regimens exist, and professional guidelines differ based on factors such as the patient’s age, parity, and gestational age of the pregnancy. The primary goal of this review was to determine whether cervical preparation is necessary in the first trimester and, if so, to identify the most effective method. To address this, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were analyzed. These trials investigated pharmacologic or mechanical methods of cervical preparation, excluding nitric oxide donors, which were reviewed separately. The outcomes assessed included the degree of cervical dilation achieved, the duration and difficulty of the procedure, side effects, patient satisfaction, and adverse events. A total of 51 studies were included in the analysis, encompassing 24 different comparisons of cervical preparation methods. The results were reported as odds ratios (OR) for categorical outcomes and weighted mean differences for continuous data. When compared to placebo, several agents demonstrated significant effects in cervical preparation. These included misoprostol (400–600 µg administered vaginally or sublingually), gemeprost, mifepristone (200 or 600 mg), and prostaglandin E and F2α (2.5 mg administered intracervically). Among these, misoprostol was found to be more effective than gemeprost in preparing the cervix and was associated with fewer gastrointestinal side effects. The timing and route of administration of misoprostol influenced its effectiveness. Vaginal administration of misoprostol 3 hours before the procedure was more effective than administration 2 hours prior. Additionally, vaginal administration resulted in greater initial cervical dilation and fewer side effects compared to oral administration. However, sublingual administration of misoprostol 2–3 hours before the procedure showed superior cervical effects compared to vaginal administration. When comparing misoprostol to mifepristone, misoprostol (600 µg orally or 800 µg vaginally) was less effective than mifepristone (200 mg administered 24 hours before the procedure) in cervical preparation. Similarly, when compared to day-prior laminaria tents, vaginal misoprostol (200 or 400 µg) showed no significant differences in the need for additional mechanical dilation or the duration of the procedure. Osmotic dilators such as Lamicel and Dilapan were comparable to gemeprost in terms of cervical ripening, although gemeprost was more effective than laminaria tents. Older prostaglandin regimens, such as sulprostone and prostaglandin E2 and F2α, were associated with higher rates of gastrointestinal side effects and unplanned pregnancy expulsions. Few studies reported on women’s satisfaction with the various cervical preparation techniques. In conclusion, modern methods of cervical preparation are generally safe, though their efficacy and side effect profiles vary. Adverse events such as cervical laceration or uterine perforation are rare, and no studies have specifically examined whether cervical preparation impacts these outcomes. Cervical preparation reduces the duration of the abortion procedure, which becomes increasingly important as gestational age advances, given the greater difficulty and time required for mechanical dilation at later stages. However, the data do not identify a specific gestational age at which the benefits of cervical preparation outweigh the associated side effects, such as pain or the delay in completing the procedure. Among the available methods, mifepristone (200 mg), osmotic dilators, and misoprostol (400 µg administered vaginally or sublingually) are the most effective options for cervical preparation.
